newsitem.title: USA: Clothing maker VF to invest $1.25 billion.
newsitem.headline: Clothing maker VF to invest $1.25 billion.

text.p: Clothing maker VF Corp., whose brands include Wrangler and Lee jeans, reported record profits Tuesday and said it would spend $1.25 billion over the next four years to improve sales.

VF, the world's largest publicly held clothing maker, also said it expected another record year in 1997 with growth of 8 percent to 10 percent. Privately held Jeans maker Levi Strauss & Co. is the world's largest brand-name clothing maker.

Wyomissing, Pa.-based VF said it plans to invest $150 million in a reorganization intended to free up resources for its $1.25 billion programme of factory consolidations, consumer research, marketing and other efforts.
The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the reorganization would cost 2,000 to 3,000 employees their jobs, but VF's statement made no mention of job cuts.
A VF spokeswoman said she had no knowledge of any upcoming job cuts. She said the programme was designed to create $2 billion in new annual sales by the year 2000, which would create jobs.

VF posted record fourth-quarter net income of $82.7 million, or $1.28 per share, compared with a loss of $35.6 million, or 57 cents per share, in the 1995 quarter. The 1995 results included a charge of $155.9 million, for realigning factories, cutting administrative expenses and revaluing inventories.
Net income for the year was a record $299.5 million, or $4.64 per share, vs. 1995 profits of $157.3 million, or $2.41 a share.

VF, which also makes intimate apparel, sportswear and work clothes and whose other brands include Jantzen, JanSport, Vanity Fair and Healthtex, reported record quarterly and annual sales along with the record profits.
Fourth-quarter sales rose 8 percent to $1.38 billion from $1.27 billion. For the year, sales climbed 1.6 percent to $5.14 billion from $5.06 billion.
The quarterly and annual results topped Wall Street analysts' expectations, and VF stock rose 87.5 cents to $68.875 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

"We're pleased to see that the actions we took last year -- to increase brand investment, to reduce costs and to better balance our manufacturing base -- have paid off so strongly," Chief Executive Mackey McDonald said in a statement.

"Record levels of cash flow and the lowest debt to capital ratio in 13 years give us an unparalleled flexibility to round out our portfolio via acquisitions, to repurchase shares and to continue our track record of steady increases in dividends.
"We are particularly pleased with the results of the most recent quarter, in which we booked our strongest sales increase all year," he continued.
McDonald said VF would make "an uprecedented push" with its $1.25 billion investment in its strongest products: denim clothing, intimate apparel, work clothes and backpacks.
"Over the next four years, we intend to invest a total of $1.25 billion behind our brands, including a $250 million" in consumer research, product development and marketing," he said.

"That strategy ... is also the driving force behind our move to a new, more efficient organisational structure, one that is designed to keep our brands closer to consumers and free up resources for our brand investments," he said.
As part of the reorganization, McDonald said VF will consolidate its 17 divisions into five units.
The company already has established a central office in Greensboro, N.C., to handle financial operations for all domestic units, he said.

"Despite these actions -- aggressive brand investment, a new organisation, systems and processes -- we still expect a record year in 1997 and growth consistent with our long-term objective of 8 percent to 10 percent annually," McDonald said.
